utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Before the witness will be brought in, I would briefly raise some -- two matters. One or two documents tendered through Witness Hagland. I was told that there are -- there's one document which have two P numbers. This is just in duplication, and I would like to invite the Prosecution to put it on the record how to deal with this document. Are you able to do that, Mr. Thayer, or will you do it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence and everyone. Ms. Stewart is writing furiously. If you bear with us for about ten seconds, she'll have the answer. And I think we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I can raise the other matter. Last year, before the winter recess, we invited the Prosecution to update us with the estimation of the length of the Prosecution case. We got the message that the Prosecution is considering the withdrawal of some witnesses and some other measures. I would like to ask the Prosecution to provide us with a view at the beginning of the hearing on Monday, next Monday, so that we have an update and have an idea about the length of the Prosecution case. There's no need to discuss it at the moment, but the first matter, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. P1331 can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be managed by the Registry. Now the witness shall be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Joseph. Welcome back, hopefully the last time. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I hope and I say to the Prosecution as well that we can finish with the examination of this witness quite soon, at least during the first session today. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish a good day to all those present, and God's peace unto this home and may His will be done in these proceedings and not mine, and I wish a good afternoon to the witness and wish him a pleasant stay with us. Could we now have in e-court 1D609, please, and I will have some questions relating to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. The number is not correctly recorded. Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D609. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, you told us about your proposal for demilitarisation. What I'm showing you now is a booklet on war law or the law of war for the armed forces, and therein is provided the definition of demilitarised zones. Now, my question for you is this: When you set forth -- when you put your proposal to Alija Izetbegovic, what did he reply? How did he respond to that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to the Chamber and as well to the accused and his attorney, and thank you for the good wishes. I'm going to answer in -- in two parts, because you raised our proposal again, and it was the concluding testimony yesterday but just before we closed, and I was asked to be sure that I addressed your question, and I want to be very, very clear for the record about this proposal. The question that we closed on yesterday was why would David Harland and I propose NATO air-strikes as an inducement for the Serbs to accept this demilitarised zone if, as General Tolimir points out, the Serbs had already accepted that, and I need to be, if the Court please, just to explain very simply. The reason we felt compelled to include that inducement on NATO air-strikes was because we doubted that the Serbs who were poised to vanquish the -- and take this territory and empty this enclave would accept a simple proposal for demilitarisation. Here they had entered and were poised to take the second of the three eastern enclaves, the first being Srebrenica, and simply coming to them and saying, "Wait. We'll make sure it's demilitarised. Would you please withdraw?" We doubted very seriously that they would do that when they were poised to achieve a much greater objective, which would be actually taking the territory and emptying it of its Bosniak population. And the reason why -- what's important here for the context for the Chamber to understand is when we use the term "enclave," it's important to remember that the only reason these - Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde - were even enclaves in that sense is because the surrounding Muslim majority population had already been expelled, and so this was a crucial strategic objective for the Serbs, and so therefore simply offering them demilitarisation when they were poised to take the second of three enclaves, we doubted very seriously they would accept. And just as a quick mention to Mr. Gajic and General Tolimir so they understand, I'm not singling out the Serbs here. The -- a very similar situation was in Krajina where the concentration of Serbs posed a strategic problem for Franjo Tudjman and Croatia, and that Serb population was subsequently expelled. And so that's -- I wanted to just be clear to have that answer there and to also, if the Court please, state the reason that we felt we had to have an inducement on the Bosniak side was, as General Tolimir pointed out in David Harland's report, we had suspicions about their cynicism. And I want to here offer to stipulate, as was suggested by the accused yesterday that, yes, it's quite possible is that in the negotiations over Zepa that the -- President Izetbegovic, who was apparently rebuffing the pleadings of Colonel Palic in Zepa, it's possible that they were, as David Harland's report suggested, it's possible they were cynical in their motives. We don't know that for sure, but it's quite possible that they were cynical, and it's for that reason that we included the other inducement, which was to communicate to the Bosniaks that if you refuse, then we will take that into account, we, the United Nations, will take that into account in any request for airpower. So we understood that very well, the point that the accused had raised yesterday. So it is in that context I -- I apologise for taking the Chamber's time, but I felt it necessary, and mentioning President Izetbegovic and their side, I can now answer the accused's question and say to him that, in fact, this proposal, as far as I know, was not presented to either side. It was not presented. David and I drafted it and raised it in our hierarchy, and it was -- it was not pursued. David and I, our objective there was to avert a potential catastrophe and the complete fall of Zepa and the casualties that would ensue, and who knows what would happen, and that was what David and I were trying to avert, and our proposal was -- was not then embraced by our senior leadership and my understanding is it was never proposed either to President Izetbegovic or counterparts such as Radovan Karadzic or others on the Serb side or General Mladic. Thank you, and again, thanks to the Chamber for allowing me to state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform Sarajevo of the fact that Generals Tolimir and Mladic showed interest in your proposal? Did you send this information through to Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, yes. Yes. As David Harland's reports state, I dutifully communicated our communication on the subject, and I believe that General Gobillard had a discussion with you and possibly with General Mladic as well on the issue, and I believe the fact that you and I had discussed this, and that General Gobillard and senior VRS leadership, possibly such as yourself, had discussed it. This was communicated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, I would not accept it had General Mladic not agreed to it, but he authorised me to actually give my consent, and that's why I did. Now, my second question is: Is it the case that your proposal stipulates that the Serbs would be threatened with NATO air-strikes, whereas the Muslims were to be induced to accept it? In other words, you would induce them by launching an air-strike on us, so how -- how can that be understood?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it can be understood very clearly, General, by the military reality on the situation. They were on -- had or were on the verge of capitulating. Your forces were on the verge of capturing the enclave. Our objective was very, very simple. It was to avert a potential catastrophe, to avert the casualties, both military and civilian, that would ensue, and to avert the condition of damaged survivors as we saw coming out of Srebrenica. So that was our objective, was to avert a -- another Srebrenica, and it's for that reason the military reality was such as it was. The -- the Armija in Zepa was in -- in no position to resist your forces, and the evidence for that, General Tolimir, is really in the paragraph that you read into the record yesterday from Viktor Bezruchenko's report, in which it stated very clearly, the amount of armament that the Armija had. And I'm going from memory, but I recall only two mortars there, and I don't recall any mention by -- in Mr. Bezruchenko's report of cannon, artillery, armour, or aviation assets, and you would know far better than I how many of those assets General Mladic and your colleagues on the senior VRS staff had massed around Zepa, and you know very well what would be the inevitable military outcome of -- of continuing that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was: How would you implement the proposal that you had by bombing Serbs, whereas the Serbs had already accepted the proposal? So could you give me a specific reply. Did the UNPROFOR actually consider this and how to resolve and how to actually do both these things?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the second question is: I don't know how UNPROFOR actually considered this, so again you'd have to consult others in the UNPROFOR hierarchy. I just testified that the proposal was not formally presented to President Izetbegovic, and it was, as you know, informally presented to you, General Tolimir, and also, through General Gobillard perhaps, as well to General Mladic. To answer the first part of your question, again you seem to be mystified as to why the threat was necessary upon the Serbs. The threat to bomb Serb forces, General, would be only in the situation where one side had accepted the proposal and you had refused. So as long as the VRS accepted the proposal, that is, accepted that Zepa would be demilitarised and demilitarisation, of course, would mean that your forces would have to withdraw, and that would mean, of course, General Tolimir, that the Bosniak population of Zepa would remain, and that would mean that Colonel Palic and his forces would remain, without weapons, of course, but that they would remain and that enclave would remain and that would remain in Eastern Bosnia. And whether or not that accorded with Serb objectives is something that you will know better than I. But it would be only in the situation where your side rejected demilitarisation and that you would withdraw. It would only be in that situation that you would be subject to NATO air-strikes for Zepa. As long as you accepted the terms of the proposal, there would be no -- no threat, nor would there be -- nor would NATO have been called on in that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your reply, but Mr. Joseph, as the Serbs had accepted to discuss and negotiate on this proposal, both with you and General Gobillard, why then did you bomb the Serbs after the operation was completed and after it was clear that Alija Izetbegovic was not going to accept it, because he said as much in Torlak's presence and he also said to Avdo Palic that he would not accept the disarming. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I'm sorry, I'm not clear here. When did NATO bomb Serb targets with respect to Zepa? I'm -- I don't have the right to pose a question to the -- I'm the witness, so I apologise. I'll phrase it as a statement. I don't understand a reference to NATO bombing in connection with -- with Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, you are right. It's not your position to put questions to the accused. But Mr. Thayer is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if it is the General's proposition to the witness that NATO did employ air support in connection with Zepa, then there needs to be a good-faith basis for that proposition to be laid, and I'd be curious to know what that is, since we've not heard any such evidence ever. If he's talking about some other deployment of NATO air support or power at some other time, then okay. But let's hear what we're talking about, so the witness can answer the question intelligently. Without a date, it's very unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you put your question in a way the witness is able to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, are you aware that, on the 29th of September, there were negotiations in Belgrade between Serbia's delegation and Republika Srpska delegation on their trip to Dayton? This was made public, and the Serbian patriarch also attended this meeting. Thank you. Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I can answer that specifically, General Tolimir, I'm completely confused. You're speaking about the 29th of September. I thought we were discussing events in Zepa which took place in July of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's precisely what I'm referring to, because on this day, on the 29th of September, NATO issued their threat that they would bomb Republika Srpska if they did not agree to be part of the Serbian delegation, as opposed to going to Dayton independently. I participated in those talks, and I know this for a fact. So I'm asking you, therefore, why was this threat actually -- why did it materialise, and why was Zepa and Zlovrh, why were they bombed when this was agreed on this meeting on the 29th of September, and after this the Zepa mountain and Zlovrh were also bombed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, General Tolimir. I -- my understanding was I was called before the Tribunal and this Chamber as a fact witness with respect to events in Zepa on and around the July 1995 period. The bombing by NATO that occurred in, going by memory, August and into September, I'm hazy on the dates but I believe it was August and September of that year, as you know very well was not in response to events in Zepa but, rather, in direct response to events in Sarajevo, in particular a shelling which caused numerous civilian casualties. I'm not here -- my understanding is I'm not here as a -- as an expert witness to -- to discuss those events but, rather, as a fact witness on -- on Zepa. The only context that I could supply here is -- is in that context of safe areas where you, I thought quite fairly, raised the point about weapons being in there -- in there, and I stipulated that in fact, yes, there were weapons in there and you pointed out from Mr. Bezruchenko's report that had the list. And I've just pointed out how we should also compare how that arsenal, which was probably, you and I would agree, was mostly small arms, how that would compare with your arsenal, and so that's the context in which we've been discussing this. The only thing that I can add is about this question you seem to be quite concerned about, and I know it was a major preoccupation for the VRS and the Serb -- the RS leadership during the war. The only context that I could supply, General, is the basic context where the United Nations had -- the Security Council had, much earlier, imposed an arms embargo on the entire former Yugoslavia, and as you know, that left in place the substantial arms advantage in your favour, that is, in the VRS favour, including, in particular, heavy weapons. And it was in the context of that arms embargo that eventually, following developments in Srebrenica in 1993, the Security Council put forward the safe area Resolution which allowed the United Nations to call on NATO air-strikes. And as you raised, it appeared at times that the Bosniak leadership, under President Izetbegovic, might have been cynically allowing, for example, situations of trying to exploit it so that -- so that airpower might be called upon, so that NATO airpower. And I affirm for you that there was cynicism on the part and that -- and that doing so cynically and -- and putting one's population, perhaps, at risk for political objectives, is wrong. That would be wrong. But the context here is -- the relevant context is there was an arms embargo and that that left in place this very substantial arms advantage in -- in your favour, and people like David Harland and I and General Smith and others were in the middle, trying to mitigate the damage and trying to ensure that casualties on all three sides were -- were minimised. And so that, I believe, hopefully, provides the necessary context, and perhaps we can move to a different line of inquiry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my question: Did you know that Zlovrh was bombed after there were no more Muslim forces in Zepa, and Zlovrh is close to Zepa. There are a couple of dozen Serb soldiers there. And that this was done at a time when negotiations were taking place related to the Dayton and delegations were being put together?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I would very respectfully point to my previous answer. I'm here as a fact witness with respect, most precisely and most directly, with events in Zepa of July 1995. I am not directly familiar with the targeting that NATO working with UNPROFOR employed the following month and in August. We should be very clear, Zepa had -- was completely taken by your forces in July of 1995, and so the safe area no longer existed. There was no Bosniak population there. As you have pointed out yesterday, the Armija population had fled, you pointed out in a report that where Mr. Bezruchenko had provided that in great detail. So that issue -- the enclave had been taken by your side, vanquished, and I can't really shed light on NATO targeting in the following month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a very brief question to you and I would be happy to get a brief answer. If we are talking about NATO air-strikes in August or September 1995, were you, in any way, involved in the decision-making in the NATO or in the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This proposal of yours with about the use of NATO aviation and the threats to the sides, was it just a prelude to the NATO strikes which followed in August and September? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if the Security Council, at any point in time, gave their consent to use NATO against the VRS through strikes, air-strikes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The record and the decision-making of the United Nations Security Council is a matter of record on beginning, my recollection is with developments in Srebrenica in 1993, and there were a number of UN Security Council Resolutions on that that spoke to the employment of NATO airpower, and there were also discussions and refinements at high levels between the United Nations and NATO about how to employ that, and those are all a matter of record and I'm not here to shed any light -- any particular light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked, for the record, if you knew whether the Security Council at any point in time gave a green light to UNPROFOR to bomb Serbs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the way you've characterized this, I am very reluctant to answer directly, and I'm going to simply restate what I just said, which is the decision-making of the Security Council is completely a matter of public record. Those -- the only thing that comprises a decision is the Resolution that the Security Council issues, and that's completely a matter of public record, and the authorisation that you are asking about either existed or didn't exist, and that's a matter of record and one can simply look at their decisions and find out the answer to that. This witness does not need to, and cannot, add anything in particular about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your proposal to high authorities in the UN system, you used NATO strikes as a possibility or an inducement. What particular authority did you have to refer to anyway referring to NATO strikes? Did you have a particular authorisation from the United Nations Security Council authorising the use of NATO power in that area and in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me answer the Honourable Judge's question. We had every authority to interpret the mandate of the United Nations; we were officers of the United Nations. We were civil affairs officers. What -- what authority did we have to be in Zepa in the first place? What authority did we have to go to Zepa and -- and have communication and -- and work with General Tolimir and General Mladic, to assist in the transportation of Muslim civilians from their homes across in a line. The authority to do that stemmed from United Nations Security Council Resolutions that provided the mandate for our organisation, UNPROFOR, to be there. So that -- we had our work. Everything that we did, including conversations with -- there and working on the ground with General Tolimir, General Mladic, and Colonel Palic was all pursuant to the mandate of the United Nations that was given. And to answer this -- complete my answer, Your Honour, the mandate of UNPROFOR also, with respect to the safe areas, also included the right to call on NATO for air-strikes, and we as civil affairs officers had the right to provide and supply advice and recommendations to our hierarchy. So we -- we were -- we were totally acting within our authority. We didn't -- David Harland and I did not go in the media and call for air-strikes, and we did not send a message to NATO and say, conduct -- we simply made a recommendation in our chain in order to avert a -- another Srebrenica. I hope, Your Honour, that I've answered the question. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: You have. All I wanted was a specific reference to a specific United Nations Resolution if you have one, and if you don't, just say you don't have, but that's all I wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. I didn't know you wanted a reference to a specific Resolution. The -- the safe area Resolutions began in 1993. I don't recall the numbers any more. At the time David and I had them and we had copies of them there, but they were there. They were refined periodically. The Security Council had identified, I believe, six or seven locations, including the three eastern enclaves that were considered safe areas and Zepa was -- was one of those, and we were very cognisant of that -- those Resolutions and what they were when we drafted what was a proposal, but it was a recommendation to our senior authorities to, here you go, here's a proposal that could avert a potential catastrophe and the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to Her Honour Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the framework for your activity was the Security Council Resolutions, and you mentioned 836 and 998 as the Security Council Resolutions in your statement. My question is do these Resolution allow for the use of force by NATO against the warring parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I didn't mention those specific Resolutions, you did, and that's a contribution to the record here, and I'm going by memory. It would be a lot better to review them, but going by memory, I believe they were adopted under chapter 7, and I believe they did authorise in some degree, but to be sure, I would have to review them, and anyone could review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are speaking for the sake of the record, let us look at your proposal once more, which is document 65 ter 2438, page 13 in English and 15 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we still have one document on the screen, but in fact you didn't use it with the witness; is that correct? We only saw the first page, but the discussion was not related to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll look at page 4. We'll shorten our examination since -- it doesn't matter if the witness is a Prosecution witness or mine. The witness is supposed to testify about facts. Can we have page 4. My apologies. Thank you, Mr. President, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So there on page 4, it reads "Definition of a demilitarised zone." This is, of course, a definition under international law. It reads: "A demilitarised zone represents an area which meets the following terms," and I have to read this out because we don't have a translation: "(a) all combatants have been evacuated as well as portable weapons and portable military equipment." That's one condition. Second condition: "(b) no enemy use of fixed military installations or institutions was effected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please excuse me, but I just wanted to ask what is it about this document? I didn't want to invite you to deal with this document if you wanted to have another document on the screen and put questions to the witness. You have a limited time, and it takes always time to read a portion of the document. If you left already this area and was going to deal with another one, you should do, but it's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am under obligation to tell you that this is Article 60 of the Additional Protocol to the First Geneva Convention which defines safe areas as opposed to demilitarised areas, and I am reading out here what a definition of demilitarised zone or area is, because it is relevant and important for any case. It is in effect until the signatories to the Geneva Conventions and Protocols change it or modify it. So I am reading under 112, definition: "A demilitarised zone denotes an area which meets the following conditions under: "(a) where all combatants as well as portable weapons and military equipment have been evacuated. "(b) there has been no use on the part of the enemy of fixed military installations or institutions. "(c) no act of hostility has been committed by an authority or population. "(d) all the activities related to military efforts have ceased." Below that it reads: "A necessary agreement. The status of a demilitarised zone shall be confirmed by agreement among interested parties," and this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is: Was it because there had to be an agreement that you expressed this threat to be carried out by NATO and which was subsequently materialised, the threat, by NATO and UNPROFOR. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I believe I have already testified that air-strikes that occurred the following month were as a result of shelling that was determined by UNPROFOR, and you can question General Smith, if you have any questions about this, directly, was determined by UNPROFOR to be shelling from your side that killed dozens of civilians at a market in Sarajevo, and that was the triggering mechanism for the air-strikes that occurred, and it had -- I -- I had nothing to do whatsoever with anything that David Harland and I wrote and had everything to do with the actions of your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the record, can you be specific and tell us when it was that our forces opened fire on Sarajevo causing casualties? When was it? Was it Markale? Can you remember the date or not, or was it -- was it this event that motivated the attacks on Serbs six months later?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite confused now about the question and the mention of attacks on Serbs six months later, because the war was over six months after that. The war was finished. The Dayton agreement was signed in November. So I'm confused about the reference to six months. And I've already stated I'm not here to testify about the events and the call for air-strikes in September. I've -- I've repeatedly testified. I've told you what I know. I've provided the context that I thought was helpful for the Chamber, and whatever line is attempting to be introduced here, it's not the role of this witness to either dispute or affirm it. So we've reached the limits of my ability to be helpful with you here, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have ten minutes left. You are going to deal with another -- with --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I am talking. I am talking. Please wait. You have ten minutes left, and you are just going to call another document which probably has something to do with this witness and his knowledge. You should use the last ten minutes in an appropriate time -- in an appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If we look at the document we have on our screen, and I'll read it out since there's no translation. Under (a) it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you didn't listen to my guidance. You have ten minutes left. You wanted to talk to another document which has something to do with this witness. He clarified that he can't testify about this context with this [indiscernible]. You should bear that in mind and not read into the record. This is available.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you, but this has nothing to do with Sarajevo. It's got to do with the demilitarised zone of Zepa. With full respect of Their Honours, I will not be putting questions any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't agree with this comment. I didn't stop your cross-examination. I gave you guidance to use the final time in the best way in your interest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thank the witness. I have no further questions of him. Thank you for coming here. Thank you to the Presiding Judge and everyone present in the courtroom, and -- and I apologise to all those I may have irked with my questioning, and I also apologise to Her Honour Judge Nyambe who I interrupted as she was waiting for the witness's answer yesterday. Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you. Mr. Joseph, I wish you a safe journey. God bless you, and I -- you have my best wishes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is your decision to -- to conclude your cross-examination in this way you did. I wanted to invite you, that was my guidance, to put questions to the witness in relation to a document you asked for on page 16, line 13. You wanted to put questions in relation to the document 65 ter 2438, and this is the packet containing reports by David Harland, and I think, in relation to this witness, but it's your decision in which way -- whether you want to conclude your cross-examination. Do you have questions in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any questions in relation to that other document. The document lists the numbers of the Resolutions Mr. Joseph referred to in his proposal. I stated what these Resolutions were for the record, and I put my question as to whether they empowered NATO to employ force against any of the warring parties. I have completed my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One final question. Do you tender the document 1D609?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll be grateful if you admit it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. It will marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document under 65 ter number 1D00609 will be assigned D00180, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yesterday, General Tolimir asked you if UNPROFOR had a double standard about the use of airpower. This was at transcript page 10710. And you noted that one needs the proper context to answer that question, and you pointed out that when NATO conducted air-strikes earlier in 1995, that resulted in the VRS taking peacekeepers hostage. That was on the same page of yesterday's transcript. Do you recall that testimony and those questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You referred, during the course of your answers to those questions, to the shelling of Tuzla town during the course of these events, and you mentioned that it killed about 70 people, a number of them young people, and General Tolimir repeatedly suggested to you that that shelling occurred in August. Your recollection was that it was April or May, and then I think you said April, but it would be easy to find out what the date was. Do you remember all that testimony from yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm going to slow down. I predict some trouble with the interpretation based on our speed so I will slow down, again, because we speak the same language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection. My question was in what way were the May events related to those in June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In July, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So then I asked the witness when these events had transpired. Was it in July, August, or May to see that there was this five or six-months interval between those events and Srebrenica. So my question only wanted to elicit what his memory of these events was, nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, it is always helpful to have a reference to the page number of yesterday's transcript. Then we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I provided that, Mr. President, it's at 10710. The accused repeated references to August is at 10711.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could have P756 on e-court, I'd like to clarify this issue of when this shelling of Tuzla that you testified about yesterday took place. Do you see a document on the screen before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can see that the date is the 7th of June, 1995. The author is Ken Biser and the acronym after his name is SCVAO. Can you tell us who Ken Biser is and what his position was in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ken Biser at that time was senior civil affairs officer in Tuzla. That is a civil affairs colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see here that the subject is "Tuzla incident," and if we look at the message it says, "Following is the initial report with a suspected location and an UNMO report with their initial crater analysis." If we could go to the second page in both versions, please. And we'll need to go to the third page in the B/C/S. Thank you. Sir, this report is headed "Shelling of TAB." Can you tell us what that acronym stands for.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuzla Air Base, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The heading is "Shelling of TAB Tuzla Air Base and Tuzla Old Town 25 May 1995." It states: "As a sequel to air-strikes administered by NATO at Pale Ammo dump, BSA resorted to massive retaliatory artillery shelling against Tuzla town and Tuzla Air Base, which is considered deliberate targeting of UN troops and Tuzla safe area. The shelling commenced at 1910 hours simultaneously at Tuzla Air Base and Tuzla safe area, total of 31 impacts were recorded until 2100 hours. Out of these 13 impacted in and around Tuzla Air Base, rounds falling within 500 metres to 2.5 kilometres of the base." I want to focus on this last portion, sir: "The remaining 18 impacted around Tuzla and Zivinic area. One out of them hit old part of Tuzla city centre, a place where young people flock together, as a consequence 66 people were massacred to death and 170 were wounded, amongst them 31 were critically injured." My question to you, sir: Is this date of 25 May -- well, let me start first. Did the events described in this passage, the shelling of Tuzla city centre, the old part where young people flocked together, 66 people massacred, 170 wounded, to your recollection is this the same event which you were describing to General Tolimir earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might -- it might well have been -- it might well have been that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other shelling of old Tuzla town which resulted in mass casualties of civilians, including young people, as you described yourself in your testimony? Are you aware of any other shelling in 1995 of Tuzla town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- there might have been other shelling, but that caused this many casualties, no, I'm not, and therefore this is, in fact, the incident that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to another topic that General Tolimir addressed yesterday. And, again, I'm going to try to slow down and provide some pauses between us. General Tolimir suggested to you yesterday that the Armija, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim army, attacked UNPROFOR on the 20th of July, and he further suggested to you, and this is at transcript page 10715 to 10716, that that attack, in his words, and I quote, "Marked the beginning of combat activities directed outside from the enclave." Now, this topic also ties in, I think, and we'll try to kill two birds with one stone, into your answer to one of Honourable Judge Nyambe's questions yesterday, where you noted that in order to properly answer General Tolimir's question and I'm quoting you now, "We would have to bear in mind when bombardment commenced," and that was at transcript page 10720. What I want to do is nail down some of the dates in this regard, and I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a short moment. Mr. Tolimir wants to have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't say that the posterior events came after the anterior events as Mr. Thayer put it. What I said was that the attack on the Zepa enclave was the beginning of the cessation of hostilities and the violation of the agreement that Torlak signed with the Serbian side, and that was the agreement on the basis of which Mr. Joseph arrived at Zepa. I would like to be quoted more precisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The -- to be very precise, in your question yesterday, you said, I quote: "Did the attack of the 20th of July, the attack carried out by the BH Army on the UNPROFOR in Zepa represent a breach of the agreement that had been signed and can you also tell me whether that marked the beginning of the combat activities directed outside from the enclave, including the attack on the UNPROFOR?" That was the question. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I would like to do, sir, is start off by showing you a document which General Tolimir used with you yesterday. This is 65 ter 2438, and we're going to be going to tab 3 of this document, which is at page 9 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, if I'm counting my pages correctly. Okay. I see that we've got both the B/C/S and the English up. If we could advance one page. For the record, we can see we're at tab 3 of this packet of reports. We have here a fax transmittal sheet. It's a cover page. Let's go to the next page. And we see that this is a memo from David -- a report from David Harland dated the 21st of July, but if we go forward two more pages we'll see your demilitarisation agreement that we've been talking so much about. There we go, that's it in English. And one more page in B/C/S and I think we'll have it. Okay. The first thing I'd like to do is just follow up on one question General Tolimir had for you. I think he said in his question to you that in your testimony you had referred to several Security Council Resolutions and you corrected him and said that you don't recall having testified about that. I presume what he meant to say, and I think he mentioned this towards the end, was that this demilitarisation agreement refers to several Security Council Resolutions. Do you see those Resolutions listed in this demilitarisation agreement, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and these are, in fact, the Resolutions that, in answer to Honourable Judge Nyambe's question, when I said that that at the time we had these very fresh and had them in printouts with us, in fact, this does refresh my memory and those were the Resolutions that we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this document, this report, is dated on the 19th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in fact, that's what I would like to focus on for the next series of questions, sir, is the date here. We see that it's the 19th of July, and if we look down at this document where it says, "Situation," we can see that it says you and Mr. Harland had drafted this. "Bosnian Serb forces continue to bombard the safe area of Zepa and its civilian population with heavy weapons and continue to make armed incursions into the safe area. These actions are being taken in defiance of the Security Council," and then you refer to those two Resolutions above. You and Mr. Harland in this proposal go on, we can see the two following paragraphs. I won't burden the record by reading them in, but if you take a moment, reacquaint yourself. The VRS forces have attacked UNPROFOR. At the same time, the Armija has threatened to use the Ukrainian peacekeepers as human shields. Okay. You've testified consistently that this was on the 19th. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, given that you're reporting here that the VRS has continued to bombard the safe area and its civilian population, and this is on the 19th, what were the types of sources for this information that you included here, that the civilian population and UN peacekeepers had been attacked by the Serbs? Can you tell the Trial Chamber, just generally speaking, what were the type of sources that you would have relied on to make this statement in this proposed demilitarisation agreement, that the civilian population and UN were being attacked by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to a specific source but the question asks for in general, we would have had reports from the Ukrainians in Zepa, from the Ukrainian UNPROFOR detachment in Zepa and any other UNPROFOR assets there that might have been what were termed the JCOs. They might have also sent reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at a couple of reports, including Ukrainian reports, very quickly and see how this corresponds or not with your recollection of what was being reported to you and included in that 19 July demilitarisation agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have P00583, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document on your screen, an UNPROFOR document, dated 2 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can see that it's from Mr. Harland, and the subject is "Sector Sarajevo, Weekly Situation Report." Can you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what were these weekly situation reports, and what was the purpose of them within, in particular, focusing on the civil affairs office that you were in.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports would aggregate the key developments in the -- one's area of responsibility, both military and civilian, and especially military developments that would have an impact on the overall security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just focusing for a brief moment on this first page where we see the heading, "Highlights." Do you see the portion where it says: "The Serbs have bombarded the UNPROFOR base in Zepa, and have said that they will continue until UNPROFOR leaves the pocket." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's the third bullet point.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that. Third bullet point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to page 4, if we would, please, in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The subject matter on which Mr. Thayer is now questioning the witness was not the subject matter of either examination-in-chief or the cross-examination. Furthermore, we haven't seen any document from the UNPROFOR saying that the Serbs targeted them. The Serbs never targeted the UNPROFOR and I would like that to be taken into account. Thank you. What I was talking about on two occasions were the attacks of Muslims on the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript cites that I've already provided to the Trial Chamber, as well as several lines of General Tolimir's cross-examination over the last two days have clearly gone to the issue of when the bombardment began, who began the bombardment, was there bombardment at a particular time and by whom? What I am showing the witness and what I think we will be able to accomplish in this redirect is to establish specific dates which underlie the documents which the Trial Chamber has already seen. So we get a clear record and an evidentiary record based on the very types of reports that General Tolimir just asked for. As I said, we will see Ukrainian reports, and we will find out from the witness to what degree these reports underscored or underlaid the statements that he made in his own reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is a fair conduct of re-examination related to threats and bombardment on the UNPROFOR. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Thayer could have asked the witness about this topic in his examination-in-chief. I think that there is no basis for this questioning as part of redirect, because this was not the subject matter of examination-in-chief or cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have ruled on that. Mr. Thayer explained and gave a reference to your -- the cross-examination, and I ruled on that, and let him carry out his examination. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention to the portion of this page that's headed "Ultimatum in Zepa." The first line, as we can see, states that: "The Serbs have been bombarding the UNPROFOR facilities in the Zepa enclave. "On Tuesday (27 June), most of the UNPROFOR observation posts around the perimeter of Zepa were targeted by Serb mortars, as was the company base in the middle of the pocket. On Friday (30 June), the bombardment resumed with the company base taking three direct impacts. A Ukrainian APC was destroyed and there was other damage to the compound, but there were no UNPROFOR casualties. "The commander of the Ukrainian company was told by the local Serb commander that the attacks would continue until UNPROFOR agreed to leave the pocket altogether. The harassment of UNPROFOR may be a prelude to a general assault on the enclave." Now, again, sir, this is very specific information that's being provided by Mr. Harland of your office. Tell the Trial Chamber in your experience what the basis for these types of statements, this specificity of information, was.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer for the Chamber and restate the same proviso I had when asked about Mr. Harland's report and Mr. Bezruchenko's report that I had for the accused, to state that, of course, the obvious, that this is the report of David Harland, not mine. David and I are close colleagues, and I would say -- add in general that I had the highest regard, without exception, for David Harland's ability and his integrity. I state that for the record. And to answer specifically the basis for what were David's reports, so I can't be a hundred per cent precise here, but the -- David was very, very careful and thorough, and he would have had access to UNPROFOR reporting of a nature that I've described, both from the Ukrainian, and if there was a JCO detachment there he would have had access to that and he had a very close and good relationship with the UNPROFOR military chain that would have received those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see here in the same paragraph Mr. Thayer read into the record that the commander of the Ukrainian company was told by the local Serb commander and so on and so forth. Do you recall who was the local Serb commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- going from memory there, it might have been Kusic. That might have been who the reference there, but I can't be a hundred per cent certain with that reference could be. But that could be the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I see we have five minutes until the next break. I think it would be helpful to save a little bit of time if we took the break now, just a couple minutes early, and I might be able to reduce my examination a bit and cut out some documents and focus on one or two in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the time you need for conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, Mr. President, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a different proposal. You should try to finish now before the break, because the next witness will have protective measures, and during the break everything can be prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll cut as I go. Okay. I've cut a few documents. Here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, again focusing on these events, on or about the 19th and 20th, again the demilitarisation agreement we just saw was dated the 19th, you've testified that on your first trip to Zepa during these events, and this is at transcript page 14162 to 163 of the Popovic transcript, which has now been marked as P1949 in evidence, on the first trip you were there, you testified previously that you'd been there for a while and I quote: "Towards the latter part there, after we'd been there for some time and nothing had transpired, we then heard the onset of cannon fire outgoing from nearby us, ammunitions firing, and General Mladic and others, he had gotten up and was talking to some of his guys, but I recall him suddenly becoming very serious and then the demeanour from friendly changed to rather dismissive and we were told to get out. Get out." That's in quotes in the transcript. "And this was as this firing had commenced." You further testified that: "It was coming from where we were there, positions there. This was outgoing from nearby us, the Serb positions nearby us," and you added that, "I couldn't visibly see the direction, but it was rather clear to us that this was outgoing fire towards the target below of Zepa." And then I won't read the rest in, but just to refamiliarise yourself with these events, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, to assist the witness, on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall those events on that first visit, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'd like to do is go back in this document 2438, the packet of Mr. Harland's reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher is asked to help the witness with the water. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Would it be possible to state what is the basis for this redirect examination on which this topic is now being discussed when this topic was not mentioned in either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We haven't had the question yet by Mr. Thayer, and then we can figure out that. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it will be abundantly clear, and I'd rather not state where I'm going with the witness in front of the witness at this point as I think you'll see. I just want to make sure that his recollection remains his recollection. So if we could go to 2438, please, 65 ter 2438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was used during examination-in-chief and in cross-examination several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I want to focus on tab 2, which is page 6 of both the English and the B/C/S. Thank you very much. And if we can go one page. I note for the record we can see tab 2 here on the screen. If we can go one page in each.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, General Tolimir used this report with you yesterday, and what we see here, sir, is a report dated the 20th of July, and if we can focus on the portion that mentions you and Mr. Bezruchenko, and we'll need to go to the next page in B/C/S and just scroll down a teeny bit in the English, please, we can see from the document on its face that Mr. Harland is writing about events that took place on this day, the 20th of July, he says at the top at about 10.00 a.m. this morning, and in the portion that deals with you, sir, we can see it says: "Later in the day, civil affairs officer Bezruchenko and Joseph met with General Mladic." Do you see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And again I won't read through what this report says Mladic told you, but if we could go to the next page in English. We can stay where we are in B/C/S. We can see that it says: "Mladic stated that his forces would resume their attack on the pocket at 7.00 p.m. this evening, if the Bosnians had not agreed his terms." Is that an accurate reflection of what transpired when you were there with Mr. Bezruchenko, sir, as stated here in Mr. Harland's report, Mladic stated that his forces would resume their attack on the pocket at 1900 hours that evening if the Bosnians had not agreed his terms?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Waiting for the translation. I want to be very precise for the Chamber. I have vivid memory of the bombardment, the ordnance, and General Mladic's sudden change in his demeanour. I can't recall at this time Mladic's precise words, so I cannot at this time recall whether it was precisely this formulation that Mladic relayed to us and that that formed the basis of David's reports. Again, I just restate that David was extremely careful with his reporting. We might well have been the source, but I can't at this time, 15 and a half years later, precisely recall that it was in this formulation that -- that we received this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look down two paragraphs where it says: "Just after 7.00 p.m., I received a message from Zepa that the Serbs had resumed a heavy bombardment of the enclave, and that the UN team on the spot had been told by the Serbs to return to Sarajevo." Now, my question to you is: That UN team on the spot, who was that team that had been told to return to Sarajevo by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Viktor Bezruchenko and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This heavy bombardment that's described here, is that something you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we had heard and that was the commencement of that that coincided with being ordered to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next paragraph reflects that: "At 8.30 p.m., I," and that's Mr. Harland, "received a message from Prime Minister Silajdzic." Now, we don't need to go into the rest of that paragraph because that's not relevant for our purposes. What is relevant is the next paragraph which says: "At about the same time, the Ukrainians in Zepa reported that the Bosnian forces had begun to attack their compound with small arms, heavy machine-guns, and rocket propelled grenades." Now, you will recall yesterday that General Tolimir quoted to you from Mr. Bezruchenko's report and specifically cited a document which described the Ukrainian compound being attacked by the Armija with small arms, heavy machine-guns, and so forth, and General Tolimir put it to you that this was the commencement of combat activities. How does that fit or not fit with your recollection of events, having been there at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We at that point were only permitted to advance as far as OP 2. OP 2 was on the high ground above the village, was in a steep gorge below, heavily forested. So we did not have access to the village to witness such events, which means I'm not -- I'm not disputing that they -- I'm not suggesting that they didn't happen. I'm simply saying we -- Viktor and I at that time did not have a chance to advance down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of this report where Harland reports that at about 8.30, the Ukrainians reported that the Bosnian forces had begun to attack their compound at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- cekam prevod. I have no reason to doubt the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just two quick areas, I hope, sir. One is --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, just for the sake of the record, the last line of questioning was also relevant to General Tolimir's specific question at transcript page 10721, asking whether the witness saw any shelling carried out by the VRS on 20 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just a quick question, I hope, sir, on an issue that General Tolimir raised. He showed you D173.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have that up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can -- we can see that this is a 9 February 2005 information report, and it is the result of a telephone interview between yourself and an OTP trial attorney and an investigator. Do you remember that telephonic interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, in general terms, recall having had such an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General Tolimir asked you to look at paragraph 14, which is on page 3 of the this report and page 3 of the B/C/S as well. He read into the record the paragraph. If you don't recall, that's okay. It's in evidence, and we'll go through it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand "this very issue," what that refers to, "this very issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The issue of whether you saw General Smith in Zepa down observing the evacuation. If you don't recall, I'll just pop up the transcript on e-court and we can look at it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right this is P1949. It's the 24th of August, and we're looking for page 14285. Sorry, 14284 is where the question begins. And that's page 143 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are a couple of pages of the transcript to review. I note that -- I think the witness has a hard copy. Unfortunately, we're -- we're well into the break time. I only have one other short area to go over with the witness after this one issue. I would just perhaps renew my request that we just take the break and maybe he can read these pages so he doesn't -- we don't have to sit here while he's reading through pages of transcript he couldn't recall. I just suggest that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was too optimistic. The indicated 15 minutes are now 20 minutes, 25 minutes, but nevertheless, it's better to have the break now. I was hoping that the break would be used for setting up all the technical things for the next witness, but this is not possible, but you should try to come to an end quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will have our break now and resume at half past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the Court please, may I know what pages I'm meant to read in this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, that's 14284 through 14285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That could be done during the break. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, how many more minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think about five, Mr. President. I don't know how much with this transcript we're going to have to work, but I don't think much more than that to get through this. One never knows, but I think five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have an opportunity over the break to read transcript pages 14284 to 14285 of your Popovic testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we, again just to put this back in context, we just looked at the portion of D173 where the information report of a telephone conversation with you states that: "I can recall seeing also General Smith there observing the evacuation." I think we can save the most time that way.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my testimony in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have anything to add or subtract or do anything to it or just leave it the way it is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it reflects my understanding pretty well and my skepticism about the fact that it was reported in the original statement that General Smith was there, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't think we need to actually go through reading the rest of that transcript. The pages are on the record. The Trial Chamber can peruse those two pages at its leisure, if it hasn't already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let's move on to my last topic, sir. You mentioned this morning, in answer to a question from General Tolimir, and this was with respect to the demilitarisation agreement that you drafted and proposed on the 19th of July, you were trying to put that in some context, and you said that you doubted very seriously that the Serbs would simply withdraw their forces from Zepa without the element in the agreement of close air support being threatened. Do you remember those questions this morning -- this afternoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you stated that: "We doubted very seriously that they would do that when they were poised to achieve a much greater objective, which would be actually taking the territory and emptying it of its Bosniak population." Do you remember giving that answer this afternoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you, sir, is: These two things that you talked about in that answer, the taking of the territory and the emptying of its Bosniak or Muslim population, focusing on the second part of your answer with respect to what you said was their greater objective, emptying the enclave of its Bosniak population, is that based on your observations on the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the course of my cross-examination, I showed a document in which the general warned UNPROFOR that the zone should be demilitarised so that we do not proceed to do it, whereas here mention is made of taking control over territory, and I never talked about taking control of territories. I only talked about demilitarisation of this area. So I would appreciate it if this be handled in that manner rather than adding some qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Thayer quoted from -- from the record, where an answer of this witness was recorded. We have the quotation on the screen now, and that was in relation to taking the territory and emptying it of its Bosniak population. That was directly related to that. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, sir, with respect to this second element that -- that you refer to as being part of this much greater objective of the Serbs, the emptying of the enclave of its Bosniak population, based on what you observed on the ground, based on your relevant experience during your time there, you've referred to your experience during this war, was that removal of the civilian population, you referred to it a number of times as forcible expulsion, was that collateral to, and by that I mean is that a consequence of or a byproduct of the VRS attack on Zepa, or is it something else? And that's my last question to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my answer to the Chamber: The -- the context in which Mr. Harland and I drafted that proposal was with the understanding, both from the immediate context, which was the fall of Srebrenica just a matter of days earlier, not more than a week or so, in which the entire population was expelled -- and I shouldn't say entire population was expelled, of course. The female population and children were expelled. Obviously the male population had a different fate. But it was in the context of the immediate fall of Srebrenica in which the expulsion of population was clearly a primary -- an overriding objective of the Serb forces. And in the wider context of the war, and Mr. Harland and I had been there at that time three years, going on three years, in which the Bosniak majority population in that region of Eastern Bosnia, from Zvornik in the north to Foca in the south, those are municipalities, and every municipality in between in which the Bosniak population had, prior to the war, been the majority population, had already been expelled, and this was the genesis of the term "ethnic cleansing," and so it was abundantly clear to us in the wake of the Srebrenica events that this was the same -- the same objective would apply here in Zepa and, therefore, the objective would be the expulsion of the population, differentiated, perhaps, between male and female, and it was for that reason that we -- because it was on the verge of that that we drafted the proposal the way we did, with the incentives and disincentives to each side the way we did. If -- did I answer the specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just reading.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I might spare the Chamber's time and re-reading now on the screen, your specific question to me is it was not a byproduct. The expulsion of the population would not be a byproduct collateral to military action. It would have been an objective of military action which would have been aimed at vanquishing both the military threat that existed and expelling the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

Now you are free, finally, to return to your normal activities, and again, thank you very much. The Court usher will assist you in leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could say, Mr. President, thank you. I thank the Chamber very much. Danke Schoen. Thank you, Honourable Judge, je vous remercie. I appreciate it very much, your leadership here and the timely questions, and if I can just say after these four days here, my wish that hopefully the -- these proceedings or others will reveal what happened to those like Colonel Palic and the hodza whom we worked with in Zepa. And if I could just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I should stop you here. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to say to General Tolimir and Mr. Gajic. [Interpretation] My greetings and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Ms. Hasan. You were hiding behind the column. I couldn't see you, but welcome to the courtroom. The next witness is ready to -- to testify?

utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Just to remind you, there are still protective measures in place for you like face distortion. utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
