utterances.text: Witness, have you recently had the opportunity to listen to your testimony from the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I understand that there are some clarifications you wish to make to the evidence that you gave during that trial. If we can start off with the clarification you wish to make to the testimony you gave about the two men in Susnjari who explained that the women and children were to go to Potocari. And I'll just give the transcript reference, which is page 2313 to -- sorry, 3213 to 3215. Could you please provide the clarification you wish to give in relation to that testimony.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. These were not people from Susnjari village. We were in Susnjari. They just happened to come along the road there. The point is that when some of these people provided statement to the investigators, there were some men there. Some of them were soldiers, but I cannot really confirm that they were soldiers, because they didn't have any weapons, and they had no insignia or anything of that sort that would identify them as soldiers. True, some of them did have some parts of military uniforms, but that was about it. So some investigators mentioned that there were two soldiers there, which is probably something that they misunderstood, because the way the interview went was they would put questions to me, then I would give them some answers, and then five minutes or so later they would just write it down. So maybe that's where the error occurred. There was mention of two men. They were in uniforms or in some parts of uniforms, but they were not soldiers, or there was nothing that would explicitly identify them as soldiers, no insignia or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to your testimony on page 3215, line 23, you wanted to clarify something about the use of the term "breakthrough." Could you provide that clarification.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The word "breakthrough" can mean in daily parlance to break out of something or break through something either with some forces or through an area that may be dangerous. What I meant when I used the word "breakthrough" was not the sort of exercise that involved any military activity. So when I said we wanted to break out of the area, I meant simply traverse an area rather than engage in a military action breaking out of somewhere. So this is a term that could be understood in several different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And for the next question, it may be prudent to go into private session as the witness may identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At transcript page 3220, line 3, you provided some -- you gave some evidence about the 28th Division that you wished to clarify. Could you please provide that clarification.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have a document or something where my statement is contained, because I really don't know at this stage what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have P170 -- no, sorry, P1173 on the screen. Page 3220.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be helpful if we actually display page 3219 to start with. And that would be page 34 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should read the relevant part to the witness, if he's not able to read this text in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Question -- this is from line 18: "Q. Sir, you were living in the locality close to Srebrenica which was part of the demilitarised zone. Tell me, please, did you ever hear about the existence of a military formation called the 28th Division, under the command of Naser Oric? "A. Yes, I did know of the 28th Division, everyone knows that, but it was the Territorial Defence and that was at the beginning. Simply, everyone defended his own village until Srebrenica was demilitarised. "Q. So after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, there was no 28th Division nor Naser Oric there. "A. I'm not saying that they weren't there. Naser was there; I saw him. But as for the army, it was not there. I didn't see them." Witness, does that help you in recalling the clarification that you wish to provide to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. What I said is correct. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, we can move on. Now, taking into account the clarifications you've just provided, does the evidence that you gave in the Krstic trial, is it otherwise true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly it is accurate. The substance is correct. Perhaps there were minor errors or perhaps I misunderstood the question or didn't understand it fully, and in some other instances I could have provided better explanations, but that's all. In some places I observed that there was a question put by one of the accused which asked whether in the statement I gave to the investigators there were some additional things put to me by the investigator and my answer or my clarification wasn't good enough. As I've said today at the outset, normally the investigator would hear me out, would listen to what I have to say and would then type out my statement. In some instances, I would say something right at the beginning and would then proceed to say something else, but the investigator would write what I said at the outset at the end of the statement, and then when the statement would be read out to me, somebody would ask me about certain matters. I would say, yes, it's possible, but I wasn't quite positive about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, with that clarification, can we take it, then, that the rest of the evidence that you gave in that trial, the substance of that evidence, was accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would then offer into evidence the documents that have been provisionally given the Exhibit numbers P1172 and 1173, which is his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents will be received with these numbers, P1172 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In addition to that, I would also offer into evidence the associated exhibits which were admitted through this witness at the trial, namely the documents that also have provisional Exhibit numbers P1174, 1175, and 1176 with 1174 and 1175 being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, and the first two of them under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And with your leave, Mr. President, if I may now read the summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim. He was a member of the Bosnian Army until June or July of 1993. On 11 July 1995, in Susnjari, the witness heard two men explain that the women and children were to be sent to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. The men and -- the men and a few women stayed behind and formed a column which left to Susnjari -- sorry, which left Susnjari in the early morning hours of the 12th of July, 1995. The witness, who was situated in the middle of the column, carried with him an old hunting rifle and five to six bullets. There were others in the column who carried weapons. On the morning of the 13th of July, the witness reached an open space that was located between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba. Two thousand to 3.000 persons had congregated in this area as they could not pass the Konjevic Polje road -- sorry, Kasaba-Konjevic Polje road which was blocked by Serb units. From the surrounding woods the witness saw the Serb soldiers surround this group of people. Approximately 200 to 300 of the Muslims gathered there were killed. Those who survived were taken towards the Kasaba-Konjevic Polje road. The next day, the witness and five others managed to make their way across the Kasaba-Konjevic Polje road and towards Baljkovica. They reached Baljkovica on 18th July. Shortly after their arrival there, the witness heard shots in the vicinity and calls by the Serb army for them to surrender. With the few men he was with, the witness decided to leave and continue through the woods. On the 19th of July, the witness and these men took rest in some bushes near some Serb trenches. The Serb troops called out for them to surrender. This call was then followed by some heavy shooting over their heads and another call for them to surrender. One by one, the men surrendered. The Serb soldiers, some of whom had yellow insignia bearing the word Krajisnici or Krajisnik on the left arms of their uniforms kicked and beat them with their rifle butts as they emerged from the bushed. The men were then order to lie down on their stomachs with their hands stretched out and their heads facing the ground. Stari, the commander of the soldiers, and the soldiers themselves asked the other men where the rest of the army was. One man revealed that there were around 500 men that had stayed behind. Stari got on the radio and instructed another unit that the 500 men mentioned should be "finished off," after which he told his own soldiers that the Vukovi or the Wolves would deal with that. The witness and the men he was with were then forced to give up their documents, their valuables, and money. In turn, they were then interrogated. The first to be interrogated was a boy between the age of 15 and 16. He was asked some questions and then taken a few metres away and shot. The second in line to be interrogated was another young disabled boy. He, too, was interrogated and then taken some 3 metres away, after which a single shot was heard. In a similar fashion, the witness, who was next in turn, was interrogated and taken away. Before the soldier opened fire -- opened fire at him, the witness came across the dead body of one of the men he was with. The soldier then shot the witness in his left shoulder. Despite the injury, the witness lay as still as he could so that he would not be shot again, and as he lay there, he heard other men being taken away and shots being fired. After dark, when all the Serb soldiers had left, the witness called out to see if anyone else was alive, but he heard no response. He managed to get up, and he escaped to Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the July 1995 events, the witness lost his father, his brother, and other members of his family. He is the only surviving male in his extended family. That concludes my summary. If we may now have P1175 displayed on e-court. This document -- I apologise. The number I'm looking for is P1176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast, 1175. It should be removed from the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah, if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we may have P1176. I apologise for that error.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see on the screen before you a map that you used during your testimony in the Krstic case. Can you take a look at this map and tell us whether the dotted line on that map traces the approximate route that you took from Susnjari to Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is roughly the route. It could be some 100 to 150 metres to the left or to the right, but that would roughly be the route, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we just magnify the map a little bit so that we can see a bit closer, we can see the dotted line a bit better. Perhaps slightly closer. Thank you. And if I may ask if the court usher could provide the witness with a pen, because as -- I'm going to ask him to mark this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to place an X at the approximate location where you encountered the 2.000 to 3.000 Muslims who were gathered in the open space and then surrounded by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And on this map we can see a black circle that's shaded in near the word "Baljkovica." Can you tell us what that circle is meant to mark? Do you see the circle? It's towards the top of the map there, a black circle shaded in in a grey colour.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that circle -- what that location -- what that circle's meant to mark?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would approximately be the location where we were shot, executed. I think that would roughly be the location. I believe it was me who initially drew this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, at this point I will tender -- if I may tender this map with the witness's mark on it into evidence as the next Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked map will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that you were carrying an old hunting rifle that belonged to your father and that there were a few other people that you saw in the column who were carrying weapons. Why were you carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we carried weapons to defend ourselves, and that's a fact. If we were able to defend ourselves at all, though admittedly what I personally had was insufficient. It could not have served as a means of defence. It was a trophy weapon that we kept in our home for quite a long time. And of course it was weapons, and if we would have been able to defend ourselves, we would have defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were any of the men that were with you on the 19th of July, 1995, armed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that there were, though the situation was a very difficult one, and such was our exhaustion and hunger that it was difficult to carry weapons. If you keep on running for eight days on end, and if you come across ambushes, it didn't really matter if you carried one or not. You could find one along the way as you ran, though the problem was it was difficult to carry one. And it was difficult to defend oneself. We were in such a poor condition because of hunger and everything else that our line of vision was not -- wouldn't take us further than 20 metres. That's how it was. At any rate, we didn't really count on any sort of defence. With the sort of weapons and the number of men we had, it was impossible to mount any defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were you carrying your weapon when you were captured on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes, but by the time I was captured, I had already discarded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you were captured and you emerged from the bushes, did your captors say anything to you or about you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part these were expletives, and I was pretty much pummelled and punched. I had -- I was wearing a green shirt. They were saying, "Look at him. He's a true Balija," because I was wearing that colour shirt. But it was all happening so fast. As they were punching me, it was even difficult to listen to what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And as I understand, you were the third in line to be interrogated and subsequently shot. Can you tell us where the bullet penetrated your body.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It penetrated my left shoulder from the back and exited next to my collarbone here near my neck. I can show it to you. This happened without a doubt. The distance between me and the soldier shooting at me was perhaps 1 metre. So when you stretch out a rifle, you've got only half a metre left between him and me, some 50 centimetres. So it was a close shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The next document is under seal, and it is P1175. If we could have that displayed on our screens but not broadcast. If we could also possibly zoom in on the B/C/S version so it can be read.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, if you're familiar with this document, can you please briefly tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter of discharge from the Kalesija hospital. I received this document as I was released from the hospital -- or, rather, the infirmary, as we called it. It was at Tojsici. There was a shop that was empty at the time and was, therefore, readapted as an infirmary. There were some beds there, and it would receive the wounded arriving from Srebrenica. The physician was probably from Kalesija, because the war hospital in Kalesija was not far away from the place where I was, and the documentation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it indicates that you were admitted on the 20th of July and surgically treated for soft tissue injuries above your left clavicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 7210 displayed on the screens. That does not appear to be the correct document. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, what is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the part of my body where I was wounded. That's what I can see on this photograph, and that's how I can see the area when I look at myself in the mirror.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two days ago. Yes, two days ago. Exactly two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you please circle the scar where the bullet entered your left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it really properly. I think probably here it entered, and then the other one must be the place where it got out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we perhaps go to page 2 of -- the second page of the document. It might be slightly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you will lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't think the witness was able to see it clearly. Mr. President, if I may just approach the witness's screen to see if he can see the picture clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is sometimes a problem with -- especially that screen. If the witness would raise, perhaps he can see it more clearly. Just stand up for a little bit. Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. So this is the entry wound, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher will help you with the pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was the entry wound, and this here would be the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you mark the entry wound. Outside of that circle, could you mark it with a number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And then could you draw a circle around the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And mark that with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I offer this photograph with the witness's markings into evidence as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the original document will be added to the 65 ter exhibit list, because I didn't see any objection to that by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, after the Serb soldiers left the execution site, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I went towards the free territory, by that time in the territory controlled by the BiH Army. It was very difficult, and it's not easy to describe it. It was night-time. Before I was shot, I was able to hear certain things. For instance, I could see the defence line. That was before I was captured. And I assume that that was some sort of a line separating the Serbian Army and the BiH Army. So that's my assumption. That's something that I saw before I was shot. After that, after I was shot and while I was lying down, I heard some sounds from the mosque. So that's what enabled me to conclude that that would be probably the territory that for me would be a free territory. By that I mean the territory controlled by the BiH Army. So I continued going downwards throughout the night. It was very difficult. I was very tired. To put it simple, I had to go. On the other hand, I knew that I wouldn't be able to endure all this if it lasted any longer. I lost lots of blood, and I knew if it lasted one more day I would not survive it. So that's why I decided to cross, although there were many obstacles. It was very difficult. Shells were landing around, around me, while I was walked during the night. So I was thinking is it possible that they could see me even during the night when it was complete darkness. But then in the morning when I crossed over to the free territory, and at the time I didn't know it was the free territory, I came across a lad who was standing on top of a hill. It was fields. I didn't know who he was. I could see that he had a rifle on his shoulder, a very old rifle. It was an M-48, as we used to call it. And he was facing the direction opposite to the direction from which I was coming, so I was getting closer to him, and it was a very unpleasant situation, because I didn't know where he was. And when I came about 10 to 20 metres, I called out to him, simply to alert him to the fact that I was approaching him, and he was so much afraid that he dropped the rifle when he heard me calling out to him. So then I approached him, and I asked him who he was and where he was. He answered that he had no idea where he was. He was very sad. He said that his father and his brother were going with him during the night, that there was shelling around them, that he was caught in this crossfire, that he lost his father and his brother, and he was now trying to look around to see whether they would reappear. We stayed there for about ten minutes, and then we continued going towards the village, because we wanted to figure out where we were, whether we had arrived or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if I may just go back a little bit. How were you able to see the defence line before you had been shot?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was exactly the place where we were captured. That was a hill that looked exactly like an elevation. You know, that was really the highest point in this area. And there was some kind of trenches on that hill. Now, I wouldn't know which army made them, but I can tell you that that was the highest point there. So when we arrived there, we looked around. It was done very quickly. We didn't spend much time there. And then we could see down there at some distance, 1 kilometre or maybe 2 or 3, I really can't tell you precisely, we considered there was some sort of a field, and there were many tanks and transport vehicles, soldiers stretched out along maybe 1 or 2 kilometres. I cannot be very precise again. So you could see that that was probably their last line. On the other side you could see a mosque, and that mosque had not been destroyed. More precisely I'm talking that the spire hadn't been destroyed. So that would be some sort of a proof that that must have been under the BiH control, because if it was under the Serbian control, the spire would have been destroyed. It wasn't possible to see a spire next to a mosque if it was under Serbian control. So that was an indicator telling me that that was probably the direction into which I should be going.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the village that you arrived at?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the village was Nezuk. Now, there are two Nezuks. I learned that only later, of course. I didn't know that until I arrived there. So there is a village called Nezuk which had a mosque, and you could see that mosque from the position that we were at, and that was a Muslim village. Right next to it. It wasn't really a great distance, maybe 500 metres, maybe a thousand metres, there was also another village called Nezuk. I saw that when I came there. And I arrived exactly in that other village which was quite badly burned down. And then I went to this other Nezuk, the Nezuk containing the mosque. So first I arrived to the village which was burnt down, but it was completely empty, full of vegetation, and then later on I went to the other place. And then when local people asked me where I went, I showed them by hand, and then they told me that it was probably a Serbian Nezuk. I think that it is -- that its name is Nezuk. I think that both villages are called Nezuk, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 7211 displayed. Could we -- could we magnify the map where it says "Nezuk" in the top centre. You see Baljkovica on the left-hand side and Nezuk. A little bit closer than that. If we can go a little bit closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the orange circle there with the crescent above it? It's marked -- it's right next to "D. Nezuk."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Some sort of a red point. It marks a spot. Yes, I can see it. That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That spot with a half crescent is a marker for a mosque in the village of Nezuk, D. Nezuk. Would that have been the mosque that you heard the call to prayer from and that you saw from the hill where you were?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. If you have a marking for a mosque here, then that must be it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be added to the 65 ter exhibit list and received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1966, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to turn now to the 19th July 1995, but I note the time, and it is perhaps a good point to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is time for our second break, and I hope you will be able to finish quite soon after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have one area to cover after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourned and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hasan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall giving the names of the men you were with on the 19th of July at the execution site to the Bosnian police in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. They were mostly my family and neighbours. Maybe one of them wasn't close to me and I didn't know his exact name, but they were mostly people that I knew well. Simply put, my neighbours. Relatives as well, my father's family, my brother's child, my brother-in-law. My sister was married to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now your cross-examination. At least the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace unto this house and unto all those present here, as well as the witness, and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine. I wish him a pleasant stay with us, and a safe journey home once he has finished his testimony. Since we both speak the same language, I'd like the witness to pay attention to the transcript and to make sure that he does not start answering my question before everything has been recorded in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the outset of your testimony, at page 47, line 15, the Prosecutor asked you to give your clarification which had to do with your testimony in the Krstic case, and then at page 49, you clarified that bit about those two men telling you that you had to go to Potocari or to Susnjari. My question is this: Is this something that you said to the investigators at a time when they were taking a statement from you, because you did refer to investigators, were these the investigators the investigators of the ICTY or the investigators of the state security of the Federation who were taking a statement from you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you know, I gave more than one statement, and there are several written documents as a result. As I am now in the courtroom, I would have to look at the document in order to be able to tell you which exactly the statement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 49, line 24 of today's transcript where you say: These were not people from Susnjari. They did wear parts of military uniform, and that's probably how the investigators wrote it down. That's it. Perhaps they wore parts of uniforms, something to that effect. Do you recall that this is something you said today to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you were referring to the investigators here, did you mean the investigators of this Tribunal or some other investigators?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the statement I gave before my testimony here. There were three statements that I gave to the investigating officers in Tuzla. Each of these investigators, as they were taking a statement from me, took the information they thought was relevant, because if you took all the information of my journey between the 11th and the 20th of July, that would have to cover a lot more pages than it did. They took the information that they believed I could testify to and that they believed they needed. So they didn't take all the information I gave them. So one of them said -- please go ahead, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. That was exactly what Mr. Tolimir was asking you. Were these investigators in Tuzla investigators of the ICTY, of the Prosecution of this Tribunal, or from another institution? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they were investigators of this Tribunal. I think that the first statement was taken by a man from Lukavac who worked as an investigator at Lukavac. Now, who he worked for, I really don't know. I think he was the person I gave my first statement to, or maybe the second statement. At any rate, there were also ICTY investigators in Tuzla whom I gave a statement to as well, at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to assist Mr. Tolimir to clarify this. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at the statement that will appear on our screens in a moment, which is 65 ter 01562, which the Prosecution disclosed to the Defence, it's P1174. So can we have it on the screen, please, in order for us to clarify some issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document that's under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we only broadcast it for the benefit of the witness and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, who did you give this statement to, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the entire statement through to the end, please? If I can just browse through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. You see the bottom there. You see your signature.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is only one page of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will be going through it page by page and you will have an opportunity to see all of it. So did you give a statement to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Interior, State Security Service, SDB Tuzla, on the 26th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of August. Well, I gave this statement in the Lukavac municipality, as we can clearly see here. So I gave this statement in Lukavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So these were not ICTY investigators. This was an investigator from the state security of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you were referring to that statement you gave to the ICTY investigator, I want to refer to this statement. Can we have the second paragraph of this statement which reads, I quote -- I'm quoting from the first line of paragraph 2: "At the beginning of July of this year, at the peak of the infantry and artillery attacks by the Chetniks which were at their fiercest from the direction of Zeleni Jadar, I was on the defence lines in the area of Susnjari and Jaglic together with most of the inhabitants." This is my question: Was this a defence line or was this your village? You said earlier on that this was your village and not a defence line?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I said it. This was my village, which was at the same time on the defence line. In other words, my village was located on the defence line, and that's where I was when these two men happened upon us, or two soldiers, if you insist on this. At least that's how I understand your first question, that I'm denying that these were full-fledged soldiers. Well, I don't know that. They may have been soldiers, but there was no inscription on them. They had part of military gear on them. When I was answering to his questions, the investigator was writing what I was saying, and he may have noted it down as me saying these were soldiers or civilians. What I'm saying is they may have been soldiers, but they didn't have any insignia, and they didn't carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my next question so I will not be putting it to you but answer this first question of mine, please: Was the defence line covering every inch of your village or was it across a swathe of land, since you said earlier on that it was some 500 metres away from your home? So can you please clarify this for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's illustrate this with an example, and I'm giving you an example. When I was leaving home to attend the trial, I told my wife and my family that I was going to The Hague. In other words, I wasn't telling them the street name or the address of the Tribunal. I would have said that I was going to such and such a street on such and such a number. I said that I was going to The Hague. It so happened that my village was on the edge of this line and that there was an APC belonging to UNPROFOR which was some 500 metres away from my home, or that's to say away from my village. So it's very difficult for me to say that the line was passing along where the -- the APC was. Maybe that particular land plot had a specific name to it, but that would be something that we in the village would be privy to and not the investigators asking about it. So I didn't go into all these details because I took them for granted. When I said that the defence line was where my village was, then I meant that it was there some couple of hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with my view that a defence area is -- covers a larger area than a defence line? Were there any soldiers on this strip of land where the APC was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the troops of the BH Army or some other troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll -- it's not my place to hold any opinion. You tell us which soldiers these were.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some five soldiers accompanying this APC. Since it was 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., roughly, we didn't carry watches and weren't interested in the time of day, really, these same individuals under heavy artillery fire which you, General, probably knew was being opened, left the APC and joined the group of us locals, and they offered everything they had, the APC and their weapons, to protect us, because the fire was so heavy that it wasn't possible to discuss these matters as normally as we do here in this courtroom now. We were under heavy artillery fire, shells. You know that shells were landing nonstop. And they offered to try and help us to stop the fire, but you know that there was no Armija. There was no army. The weapons were turned over to the Dutch or Canadian Battalion. The United Nations took upon themselves the obligation to protect us, and we expected them to do so. At that point in time, there were these five soldiers on the line, and as these things were happening, a short while later they left too. So there was no line to speak of. If you can call a place where there is an APC a line, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please be brief in your answers. If you say that there was no line to speak of, then there was not one. We will not argue about it. Tell us, was there an observation post belonging to UNPROFOR? If there was no line there, were there any VRS troops opposite that line close to Susnjari, if you could see that far?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the place is Jaglici. You have the village of Jaglici, and beyond that village, some hundred metres beyond the village, there was the point where these soldiers were located. From that location as the crow flies, a thousand metres away there were VRS positions, but the Serbian Army did not engage in a breakthrough with their infantry on that day. They only opened artillery fire. They were advancing on the other side of Srebrenica, from Zeleni Jadar. The safe area was not that large, and you were able to see the village on the other side from our vantage point, especially if you see a large group of people, of refugees fleeing as the army was advancing. But there was no infantry attack to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since a moment ago you explained for Their Honours that the two persons who wore parts of uniform and of whom you said you didn't know who they belonged to, they arrived and you say, for instance in line 5: "Two soldiers arrived in Susnjari --" I'm referring to this statement of yours, paragraph 2, line 5: "Two soldiers arrived in Susnjari, unknown to me, letting the people know that the women, children, and the infirm should move to Potocari towards the UN base and the able-bodied men should embark on a breakthrough to the free territory." My question is this: Did you say as these two individuals told you to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last part of Mr. Tolimir's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that's right. At that time you couldn't seek guarantees. There wasn't much you could do. These were the very last minutes that we spent in that area. Whoever would come across us and tell us anything, we would hear them out. We would accept what they said, because we didn't have any other information. We couldn't treat them as unknown soldiers, because if anybody was truly unknown to that area, they would not even dare show their face there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, do you remember what it was you told to the ICTY investigators in relation to these two individuals? Do you remember? Was the statement identical to what you just said now or was it different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is the last question for today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you what happened. I think that I gave the same statement to everybody else. I think that all my statements are identical. Maybe some of the investigators changed a letter or a word, or maybe they didn't manage to catch everything, but all my statements are something that I stand behind, and I can state that here in public today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's time to adjourn. Sir, we must adjourn for the day, and we will resume next Monday. I apologise that you have to stay here over the weekend, but there is no other way to conclude your examination. The court usher will assist you. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume on Monday at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
